## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Sources disagree about the best wind direction.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the wave size this break works in.
- No survey or peer-reviewed study of the bottom was found.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the swell period this break needs.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Nine sources from nine publishers; eight were read directly. Surfer Today (403) is kept as web_search. The biggest change: the WSL 'What Makes Teahupo'o Tick' post is Surfline-sourced and was dropped. It was the only source with a 180-220 window, a 14-18 s period and the N/E/ESE wind. Two directly readable spot guides were added by following site indexes: Yeeew and WannaSurf. Wind: Yeeew says the ideal wind is NE (45). Surf-Forecast says NNE (22.5). Surfer Today (search evidence) says a northerly breeze keeps it glassy. All three support the profile's 30. WSL's 2015 best-conditions table says East (60 deg off) and is the only contradiction. The Conversation and Swellnet say the trade winds keep the face clean but name no direction. WannaSurf's wind field is empty. Swell direction: S (Surf-Forecast), S-SW (WSL, Surf Atlas, Yeeew), SW prevailing (Swellnet) and SSW (Surfer Today), all consistent with 190-225. Tide: all tides (Surf-Forecast, Yeeew, WannaSurf). WSL says mid is preferred but it works on all tides. The Conversation explains why: the tidal range is low. Season: winter (Surf-Forecast), May-October (Surf Atlas), storms March-November (WSL) and April-September (Surfer Today); all consistent. Period: The Conversation (Tom Shand, University of Auckland) gives 14-20 s for the arriving swell. Size: WSL's best-conditions 4-12 ft (scale not stated), WannaSurf's start at 3-5 ft and Yeeew's 'chest high to tow-in size' fit the profile's 4 ft minimum. WannaSurf says it holds 16 ft and over, and Yeeew says it gets good up to tow-in size. No source gives a numeric holding maximum, so the profile's 25 ft maximum is unsupported but not contradicted. Bathymetry is qualitative or semi-quantitative only: 51 cm over the reef (Wikipedia), about 1,000 ft deep less than half a mile out (WSL), a shelf at about 10 m (The Conversation). No survey dataset or peer-reviewed paper was found; Crossref returned nothing for Teahupo'o. The Wikipedia shape sentence ('races along into a dry reef closeout') cites Surfline's Surfing A-Z. It was kept because it is Wikipedia text with no conditions data, but it is flagged here. Republications of the Conversation article (Inverse, Swellnet, Daily Maverick and others) were not added as separate publishers.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 3–5 ft (1–1.5 m); yeeew: chest high (scale not stated) / body-relative | documented | S8, S9 | `wave_height_min_ft` 4 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | 4–12 ft (scale not stated) | documented | S3 | no separate setting; working range 4–25 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 16 ft (5 m) or more; yeeew: up to tow-in size (scale not stated) | documented | S8, S9 | `wave_height_max_ft` 25 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at 1.0-1.5 m / 3-5 ft (the page's own conversion, scale not stated) and Yeeew that it gets good from chest high (body-relative); WSL's 4-12 ft best-conditions range is recorded under ideal_range, not as a minimum.
  - S9 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “Gets good between chest high and tow in size.”
- **Ideal range**: WSL's 2015 best-conditions table gives a swell height of 4-12 ft without stating whether it is face or offshore swell height.
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Swell Height: 4' - 12'”
- **Maximum suitable**: WannaSurf says it holds up to 5 m / 16 ft and over and Yeeew that it gets good up to tow-in size and stops getting taller (only thicker) once it hits triple overhead; neither gives a closed upper limit.
  - S9 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “Gets good between chest high and tow in size.”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “Once it hits triple overhead, it stops getting taller, and just keeps getting thicker.”

### Swell period

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal | — | not documented | — | `ideal_swell_period_s` 16 s |
| Acceptable | — | not documented | — | `min_swell_period_s` 13 s (minimum) |
| Short-period behaviour | — | not documented | — | no spot-specific setting (periods below `min_swell_period_s` score lower) |
| Long-period behaviour | long-period waves start feeling the seabed only a couple of hundred metres from the reef, so they shoal very abruptly | documented | S5 | no spot-specific setting |

Notes:

- **Ideal**: No excerpt states a preferred period; The Conversation (2024) says the swell reaching Tahiti has periods of 14-20 s, which describes what arrives rather than what works best, and Surf-Forecast says only that it tends to receive distant groundswells.
- **Acceptable**: No excerpt states an acceptable range of swell periods.
- **Short-period behaviour**: No excerpt describes how the break handles short-period swell or windswell.
- **Long-period behaviour**: The Conversation (2024) says long-period waves normally start interacting with the seabed at around 200 m depth, which at Teahupo'o is only a couple of hundred metres from the reef.
  - S5 (The Conversation): “long-period waves normally start interacting with the seabed at depths of around 200 metres...But at Teahupo'o, it is much closer, just a couple of hundred metres.”

### Swell direction

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal bearing | 180–225° (S to SW, clockwise); more westerly intensifies: yes; surf forecast: 180° (S); surfer today: 202.5° (SSW) | documented | S2, S3, S4, S5, S7, S8 | `optimal_swell_direction` 190–225° (S to SW, clockwise) |

| Exposure | exposed reef break with very reliable surf; deep water runs close to the reef | documented | S2, S3 | no setting |

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives south as the best swell direction, Surfer Today (search summary) south-southwest, and Yeeew, WSL's table and Surf Atlas south to southwest, while The Conversation says more westerly swells increase the intensity of breaking.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south.”
  - S4 (Surfer Today): “The best conditions are generally a south-southwest swell, while a northern breeze will ensure its glassy look.”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “The best swells are from the South or Southwest.”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Swell Direction: South - Southwest”
  - S7 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “As the strong SW-S swells collide with the outer reef, it hits a gap of less than 20 inches between the ocean surface and the corals.”
  - S5 (The Conversation): “This happens particularly on more westerly orientated swells, increasing the intensity of breaking.”
- **Acceptable range**: No excerpt states a range of working swell directions.
- **Blocked directions**: No excerpt names swell directions that are blocked or shadowed by land or reefs.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break with very reliable surf, and WSL says the water is still about 1,000 ft deep less than half a mile out.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Teahupoo in Tahiti is an exposed reef break that has very reliable surf.”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “because the ocean stays deep close to shore -- less than a half-mile out, the water is still about 1,000 feet deep”

### Seasonality

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prime months | May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep | documented | S2, S3, S4, S7 | `best_months` Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep |

Notes:

- **Prime months**: Surfer Today (search summary) gives April to September, Surf Atlas the main SW swell season from May to October and Surf-Forecast winter, and WSL says the Antarctic storms are strongest from March to November; May to September is common to the two month ranges.
  - S4 (Surfer Today): “the best time of the year to witness epic conditions is between April and September, especially in the morning”
  - S7 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “The southern breaks are the more reliable, the heavier, and the ones that work in the main SW swell season (from May to October).”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Winter is the optimum time of year for surfing here.”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Energy from powerful maelstroms that blow over the waters off Antarctica (strongest from March to November) travels thousands of miles to arrive in the form of south and southwest swells.”
- **Secondary season**: No excerpt states a secondary or shoulder season.
- **Swell sources**: WSL says powerful storms off Antarctica send south and southwest swells, Swellnet that the Southern Ocean provides the storms, Surf-Forecast that it tends to receive distant groundswells, and The Conversation that the waves arrive as ordered swell.
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Energy from powerful maelstroms that blow over the waters off Antarctica (strongest from March to November) travels thousands of miles to arrive in the form of south and southwest swells.”
  - S6 (Swellnet): “With ever reliable trade-winds taking care of surface conditions, we rely on the Southern Ocean to provide swell-generating storms”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south.”
  - S5 (The Conversation): “By the time the waves reach Tahiti they have become ordered swell, with wave heights of two to five metres and periods of 14 to 20 seconds between successive waves.”
- **Wind patterns**: The Conversation says the wave breaks nearly opposite to the prevailing trade winds, keeping the face smooth, and Swellnet that ever-reliable trade winds take care of surface conditions; neither names a direction.
  - S5 (The Conversation): “the Teahupo'o wave breaks in a direction nearly opposite to the prevailing trade winds, keeping the wave face smooth”
  - S6 (Swellnet): “With ever reliable trade-winds taking care of surface conditions, we rely on the Southern Ocean to provide swell-generating storms”

Notes:

- **Break type**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break and Wikipedia describes an extremely shallow coral reef; no excerpt names the wave direction.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Teahupoo in Tahiti is an exposed reef break that has very reliable surf.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “An extremely shallow coral reef, which ranges up to 20 inches (51 cm) beneath the water's surface, is responsible for a very hollow-breaking wave.”
- **Orientation**: No excerpt states which way the coast or the break faces.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Teahupoo in Tahiti is an exposed reef break that has very reliable surf.”
- **Bathymetry**: Wikipedia gives up to 20 inches (51 cm) of water over a semi-circular reef that drops sharply and Surf Atlas less than 20 inches over the coral, WSL says it is about 1,000 ft deep less than half a mile out, Surfer Today (search summary) 150 ft to 6 ft over a short distance, The Conversation describes the 200 m depth contour a couple of hundred metres out, a flatter shelf at about 10 m and a deep channel alongside, and Yeeew says the bathymetry makes the water suck out hard; no survey dataset is cited.
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “An extremely shallow coral reef, which ranges up to 20 inches (51 cm) beneath the water's surface, is responsible for a very hollow-breaking wave.”
  - S7 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “it hits a gap of less than 20 inches between the ocean surface and the corals. That pushes huge amounts of water skywards”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “This is semi-circular, and drops down sharply, creating a 'below water' effect; the extreme angles in descent create an instant instability to the wave.”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “because the ocean stays deep close to shore -- less than a half-mile out, the water is still about 1,000 feet deep”
  - S4 (Surfer Today): “swells move from very deep water (150 feet) to very shallow water (six feet) over a short distance”
  - S5 (The Conversation): “long-period waves normally start interacting with the seabed at depths of around 200 metres...But at Teahupo'o, it is much closer, just a couple of hundred metres.”
  - S5 (The Conversation): “At around ten metres' depth, a flatter shelf in the reef allows the wave to stabilise and "stand up" with a steep front face, before finally breaking as the reef rises again.”
  - S5 (The Conversation): “A deep channel runs alongside the shallow reef shelf. The wave doesn't break in this deeper area, allowing it to peel”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “The nature of the bathymetry (bottom of the ocean) here makes the water in front of the wave suck out hard, so you end up surfing way below sea level.”

## Conflicting information

- **Wind · offshore**: Surf-Forecast names a north-northeast offshore, Yeeew a northeast ideal wind and Surfer Today (search summary) a northern breeze, while WSL's 2015 best-conditions table lists east.

## Judgement check

Every field's excerpts were re-read on 2026-10-27. Changes:

- swell_period.ideal: 14-20 s -> not documented; the excerpt gives the period of the swell that reaches Tahiti, not a preference.
- swell_height.min_suitable: dropped WSL's best-conditions 4 ft (the bottom of an ideal range, kept under ideal_range); WannaSurf 3-5 ft and Yeeew chest high stay.
